clue.text: Drink's temperature mostly kept cool?

indicators.note: mostly means the phrase loses its final letter, keeping the greater part

parts.note: something kept cool, like champagne, is on ice

explanation.surface: Someone wonders whether a beverage has been kept chilled for most of the time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'mostly' trims the last letter from ON ICE, the phrase for 'kept cool', leaving ONIC after T.
explanation.definitionFit: A mixer such as quinine water is a familiar example of a beverage.

clue.text: Prompt detaining outlaw: he left behind part of shoe

indicators.note: detaining means the first word holds the next pieces inside itself, as if in custody

parts.note: a cue is a prompt given to an actor
to outlaw something is to ban it
taken as written

explanation.surface: A swift arrest of a bandit, who leaves a piece of his footwear at the scene.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Prompt' reads as an adjective but is the noun for an actor's reminder, and 'outlaw' is a verb. 'detaining' is the container signal and 'behind' sends the last letter to the end.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a moderately high, straight-sided style of the raised back section on footwear.

clue.text: Troops travel in vessel, one approaching a region of S America

indicators.note: approaching sets the one right next to the letter that follows it
in places the troops and the travelling inside the word for a vessel

parts.note: a pan is a cooking vessel
TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's former volunteer reserve force
to travel is to go
I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: Soldiers sail by ship, with one of them nearing a part of South America.
explanation.walkthrough: The Territorial Army was Britain's volunteer reserve force. 'vessel' suggests a ship but is a cooking pot; 'in' is the container signal and 'approaching' only sets two letters side by side.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the sparsely populated southern end of the continent, shared by Argentina and Chile.

clue.text: Competitor back on wheels

indicators.note: back tells you to read the two pieces together from right to left

parts.note: re means on, in the sense of concerning
wheels is slang for a car

explanation.surface: A contestant returns to action on a bike or in a vehicle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'back' turns RE + CAR, read as RECAR, right to left. 'on' is not positional: it means 'concerning'.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who takes part in a speed contest is one kind of contestant.

clue.text: Faction stopping ruler going off the rails

indicators.note: something going off the rails has lost its proper course, so the letters are thrown out of order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A political clique prevents a monarch from behaving wildly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'going off the rails' rearranges all thirteen letters of STOPPING RULER.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a breakaway set of members who have left a larger party, a synonym for a dissenting clique.

clue.text: Not initially very well-behaved

indicators.note: not initially means the word loses its opening letter

parts.note: truly can mean very, as in truly sorry

explanation.surface: A child who was not very good to begin with.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not initially' removes the first letter, T, from TRULY. The answer is a rare word, the opposite of its familiar un- form.
explanation.definitionFit: A rare adjective meaning orderly and obedient, the positive of a commoner negative word.

clue.text: Cleric — a Roman Catholic — bound to admit mistake

indicators.note: to admit means the word for bound lets the mistake inside it

parts.note: to bound is to hop or leap
bish is dated British slang for a blunder

explanation.surface: A Catholic priest feels obliged to confess to an error.
explanation.walkthrough: The mistake is old British schoolboy slang for a blunder. 'bound' reads as 'obliged' but is a leap, which 'to admit' opens up.
explanation.definitionFit: A senior churchman in charge of a province is an example of a member of the clergy.

clue.text: First call up proper soldiers to take the lead

indicators.note: to take the lead puts the proper soldiers at the front, ahead of the call

parts.note: prim means stiffly proper
OR is other ranks, the British army term for soldiers who are not officers
to call someone up on the phone is to dial them

explanation.surface: An army begins by conscripting its regular troops to go in front.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to take the lead' places PRIM and OR ahead of DIAL. OR is 'other ranks', British army soldiers below officer rank. 'call up' suggests conscription but is a phone call.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym in the sense of existing from the very beginning of time, earliest.

clue.text: Eyesore among nasty edifices

indicators.note: among says the answer sits within the run of letters of the two following words

explanation.surface: One ugly building standing out among several horrible ones.
explanation.walkthrough: 'among' marks a run of letters spanning NASTY EDIFICES. 'Eyesore' is literal: a sore on the eye, not an ugly building.
explanation.definitionFit: A whimsical literal description: it is a painful swelling on the eyelid.

clue.text: Plain food items put back with dish you say I dropped

indicators.note: put back means the word for the food items is written right to left

parts.note: a menu is a list of food items

indicators.note: you say means the word for a dish is spoken and a like-sounding spelling is entered

parts.note: a dish is an attractive person, a belle
to shed something is to drop it

explanation.surface: Simple fare is returned to the kitchen along with a plate the diner admits to dropping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put back' turns MENU into UNEM; 'you say' gives BELL from the sound of BELLE. 'dish' is a good-looking person, not a plate.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym for without ornament or decoration.

clue.text: Jack is outwardly very sexy

indicators.note: outwardly says the word for very sexy goes on the outside, wrapped round the other

parts.note: hot is slang for very sexy
taken as written

explanation.surface: A man called Jack is extremely attractive on the surface.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jack' looks like a man's name but is the verb, as in jacking up a car; 'outwardly' is the container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: To jack something up is to raise or lift it with a device.

clue.text: Bait species of antelope crossing new grazing territory

indicators.note: crossing means the bait and antelope together span the new letter, which sits inside

parts.note: to bait someone is to rag or tease them
the eland is a large African antelope

explanation.surface: Lure put out for antelope moving across fresh pasture.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bait' is the verb meaning to tease, not a lure, and 'crossing' is a container signal rather than a migration.
explanation.definitionFit: It is open country used for pasturing livestock, a synonym.

clue.text: Showy flower patch concealed by front of cottage

parts.note: manor is British slang for one's own territory, especially a police district, as is patch

indicators.note: front of takes the opening letter of the word that follows

parts.note: concealed means hid

explanation.surface: A bright flower bed hidden from view by the facade of a country cottage.
explanation.walkthrough: 'front of' takes C from cottage, and 'by' sets HID beside it. MANOR and patch are both British slang for one's home turf.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a European wild bloom whose lip resembles a tiny human figure, an example.

clue.text: Nasty, wild aromatic plant

indicators.note: wild means the letters of the neighbouring word run riot into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: An unpleasant, untamed herb with a strong smell.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wild' rearranges NASTY, though it reads as describing the plant.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a strongly scented yellow-flowered herb, an example.

clue.text: Copy various pretty pics

indicators.note: various suggests the letters appear in a different, varied arrangement

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone duplicates an assortment of attractive photographs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'various' rearranges PRETTY PICS. 'Copy' reads as a verb but is the noun: text prepared for a printer.
explanation.definitionFit: Copy is a noun for typed text ready for printing, which this is.

clue.text: Egg container turned upside down

indicators.note: in a down entry, turned upside down means the word is written from bottom to top

parts.note: a tin is a metal container

explanation.surface: A box of eggs flipped over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turned upside down' inverts TIN in this down entry. 'Egg container' reads as one thing; the definition is just the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the egg of a head louse.

clue.text: Convincing fellow to support business

indicators.note: in a down entry, to support means the fellow sits underneath, holding up the business

parts.note: Co is the abbreviation for company, a business
a gent is a fellow

explanation.surface: Persuading a chap to back a company.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to support' puts GENT beneath CO in the down entry. 'Convincing' reads as a verb but is the adjective.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym for persuasive, said of a well-reasoned argument.

clue.text: Consulted judge over intervening between political opponents?

indicators.note: intervening between places the judge in the gap separating the two opponents

parts.note: Con is short for Conservative, one of a pair of political opposites
a Red is a communist or socialist, the opposite of a Conservative

indicators.note: over means the word for the judge is turned over, written the other way

parts.note: a ref, short for referee, judges a game

explanation.surface: Advice was sought from a magistrate about stepping in between rival politicians.
explanation.walkthrough: The opponents are a Conservative and a socialist. 'over' turns the judge backwards, and 'intervening between' sets him in the gap separating the pair.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym for held discussions or took counsel together.

clue.text: Cannabis and heroin featured in report …

indicators.note: featured in means the heroin appears inside the word for a report

parts.note: a report is a loud bang, as of a gun
H is slang for heroin

explanation.surface: Two drugs are mentioned in an official document.
explanation.walkthrough: 'featured in' puts H inside BANG. 'report' is the noise of a shot, not a document.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an Indian preparation of hemp leaves, a form of the drug.

clue.text: … warning briefly about a run on initially costly drug

indicators.note: about means the shortened warning goes round the other letters
briefly cuts the last letter off the word for a warning

parts.note: a notice can be a warning, as in notice to quit

indicators.note: in a down entry, on stacks the run above the letter that follows

parts.note: R is the cricket abbreviation for run

indicators.note: initially takes the opening letter of the next word

explanation.surface: A short alert about a rush on a medicine that was expensive at first.
explanation.walkthrough: 'briefly' cuts NOTICE to NOTIC, and 'about' wraps it round A, R and C ('initially' costly). The ellipsis linking it to the previous clue is only for the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: A sleep-inducing or illegal substance, a kind of the thing defined.

clue.text: Way out items of clothing in English school

indicators.note: in places the garments inside the abbreviation for school

parts.note: a cape is a garment worn over the shoulders
a hat is a garment for the head

explanation.surface: Outlandish garments worn by pupils at a school in England.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Way out' reads as 'outlandish' but is literally an exit. One plural phrase supplies two garments, which 'in' places inside the abbreviation.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an emergency exit in a ship, aircraft or submarine.

clue.text: Regularly plays reed instrument

indicators.note: regularly takes every second letter of the two words that follow

explanation.surface: A musician who often performs on a woodwind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regularly' takes the even letters of PLAYS REED. 'reed instrument' looks like one phrase, but only the last word defines.
explanation.definitionFit: It is an ancient Greek stringed harp, an example.

clue.text: Flower picked up and positioned in around a minute

indicators.note: picked up means heard by the ear, so the bloom's name is taken by its sound

parts.note: a lily is a flower
put means positioned

indicators.note: around means the word in goes round the letter after it

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A bloom is plucked and arranged in a vase in about sixty seconds.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minute' is the adjective meaning tiny, not a unit of time. 'picked up' means heard, so the bloom is respelt by its sound; 'around' is a container signal.
explanation.definitionFit: From the tiny people in Gulliver's Travels, an adjective meaning very small.

clue.text: Fork out about a pound in casual fashion? Very well

indicators.note: about means the word for fork out goes round the pound

parts.note: to fork out is to spend
L is the old symbol for a pound sterling, from the Latin libra
idly means in a casual, lazy way

explanation.surface: Someone casually pays roughly a pound and is told that is fine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps SPEND round L, the old abbreviation for a pound sterling. 'Very well' reads as grudging agreement but means excellently.
explanation.definitionFit: An adverb synonym: to do something excellently.

clue.text: Top teacher in row featured prominently in newspaper?

parts.note: head is the British short form of headteacher, a school principal
things lined up are in a row

explanation.surface: A school principal caught up in a quarrel makes the front page.
explanation.walkthrough: HEAD is British for a school principal. 'row' reads as a quarrel but is a line.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym for having been the main story at the top of a page.

clue.text: Travellers' guide much spoken of by sailor

indicators.note: by sets the sailor next to the spoken part
spoken of means the word for much is said and a like-sounding spelling entered

parts.note: loads is informal for much, a great deal
tar is an old word for a sailor

explanation.surface: A guidebook that a seaman often talks about.
explanation.walkthrough: 'spoken of' gives LODES from the sound of LOADS, and 'by' sets TAR beside it. The guide is not a book.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a heavenly body, especially the Pole Star, that navigators steer by.

clue.text: Most mature clergyman has head lowered

indicators.note: in a down entry the head is the top letter, and lowering it moves it further down the word

parts.note: a priest is a clergyman

explanation.surface: The oldest vicar bows in prayer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'has head lowered' drops the P of PRIEST two places down the entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A superlative synonym: most fully developed, as fruit or cheese.

clue.text: Lifted bed on top of hard wood

indicators.note: in a down entry, on top of places the bed above the last letter
in a down entry, lifted means the word for a bed is written upwards

parts.note: a crib is a child's bed
H is the abbreviation for hard, as on pencils

explanation.surface: A bed raised up onto a base of hardwood.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hard wood' is split: only 'wood' defines, and 'hard' is the pencil abbreviation. 'Lifted' turns the bed upwards and 'on top of' stacks it above that letter.
explanation.definitionFit: It is a type of timber from a pale-barked tree, an example.

clue.text: Hit with heavy implement? Not half

indicators.note: not half means only one half of the implement's name is kept

parts.note: a hammer is a heavy tool

explanation.surface: Struck with a hefty tool? You bet!
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not half' drops MER, the second half of HAMMER. In British speech 'Not half!' is an emphatic yes.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym as a verb meaning to strike forcefully.

clue.text: Girl soon becoming short of oxygen

indicators.note: becoming short of means the word for soon lacks the letter that follows

parts.note: anon is an old word for soon
O is the chemical symbol for oxygen

explanation.surface: A young woman will shortly run out of air.
explanation.walkthrough: 'becoming short of' takes O out of ANON.
explanation.definitionFit: A female given name, an example.
